title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
hookLine: the priests step into the Jordan first, and twelve stones are set up so children will ask "What mean ye by these stones?"

cards: The river is in flood. The book stops to tell us that: at harvest time the Jordan runs over all its banks. On the near side stands a whole people, with children, animals, everything they own.
Nobody builds a bridge. Nobody waits for the water to drop. The priests carrying the ark of the covenant walk to the edge first, and step in.
The moment their feet touch the water, the river upstream stops and stands up in a heap, and the people cross on dry ground. And before anyone moves on, Joshua asks for stones.

teach.b: Twelve men are chosen, one from each tribe. Each goes back into the riverbed, to the spot where the priests are standing, picks up a stone, and carries it out on his shoulder.
Joshua sets the twelve up at Gilgal, where they camp that night. Why? The answer is a question.
These stones are a sign, so that when your children ask in time to come, "What mean ye by these stones?" you can tell them: the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark.
The memorial is built to be asked about. A pile of river stones doesn't explain itself. Someone has to say, I'll tell you.
If that sounds familiar, it should. The Torah does the same at Passover: when your children say to you, "What mean ye by this service?"
From Egypt to the Jordan, remembering runs through a child's question and a parent's story.
The Hebrew behind in time to come is machar, the everyday word for tomorrow. The book expects the question soon, from the next generation. And there's a second pile.

teach.h: WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?
teach.b: Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, right where the priests' feet stood, and the text says they're there to this day.

teach.h: A SECOND PILE, UNDER THE WATER.
teach.b: One pile on the bank, for everyone to see and ask about. One in the river, where the crossing happened.

how: At the Passover seder the story is told in answer to children's questions, and some families keep objects at home that prompt a story to be retold.

games.q: you're one of the priests carrying the ark. the Jordan is in flood, over its banks. you're told to walk in first. what happens?
o: the water parts before you reach it.
the water stops the moment your feet touch it.
you wait on the bank until the river drops.
games.why: the river stops when the priests' feet touch the edge. they had to step into the flood before anything changed.

practice: If there's a small stone nearby, a pebble from a plant pot, pick it up; if not, any small object within reach will do.

Hold it in your palm, feel its weight, and give it one crossing from your life, a time something gave way when you didn't expect it to. Don't tell yourself the whole story; just name it, and let the stone hold it.

wordCard.voice: Twelve stones. Carried out of the Jordan, one for each tribe, and set up so that children would ask what they mean. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: what are these stones? the children's question in Joshua 4:6.

carryVoice: Your line: what mean these stones. A memory waits for someone to ask. Day seven hundred, done.
